name: Italy
description: Italy beckons expats with its unparalleled blend of rich history, vibrant culture, and world-renowned cuisine. It offers a high quality of life, a Mediterranean climate, and a slower pace of daily living, making it an attractive destination for those seeking a fulfilling lifestyle.
longdescription: Expat life in Italy is often characterized by immersion in a deeply community-oriented culture, surrounded by iconic art, architecture, and diverse landscapes ranging from snowy mountains to idyllic coastlines. While daily life can be enriched by the exceptional food and strong social connections, expats should be prepared for navigating a complex bureaucratic system that is frequently cited as a primary frustration. The economic landscape offers various opportunities, particularly in sectors like tourism, food, design, and fashion, but the local job market can be challenging, with salaries often lower than in other Western European countries. However, Italy has introduced attractive tax regimes for wealthy individuals, retirees, and workers, making it a financially viable option for specific expat profiles. The cost of living varies significantly, with major cities like Milan and Rome being more expensive, while smaller towns and southern regions offer greater affordability. Learning Italian is crucial for full social and administrative integration outside major expat hubs, although English may suffice in international business settings and tourist areas.

visas.name: Italy Job Seeker Visa
visas.description: Italy's job seeker visa allows non-EU nationals to enter Italy for up to 12 months to look for work, attending job fairs, interviews, and signing up with recruitment agencies.
benefits: Search for work in Italy
Access to the Italian job market
Schengen Area travel
Rich cultural environment
Convert to work permit if employed

visas.name: Italy Family Reunification Visa
visas.description: Italy's family reunification visa (Ricongiungimento Familiare) allows non-EU residents in Italy to bring close family members (spouse, minor children, dependent parents) to join them.
benefits: Family unity in Italy
Right to work and study
Access to Italian healthcare (SSN)
Path to permanent residency
Schengen Area travel

visas.name: Italy Working Holiday Visa
visas.description: Italy's Working Holiday Visa (Vacanza Lavoro) allows young citizens of partner countries to travel and work in Italy for up to 12 months, combining tourism with temporary employment.
benefits: Travel and work in Italy
Experience Italian culture
Schengen Area travel
Part-time or seasonal employment
No sponsorship required

visas.name: Italy Self-Employment Visa
visas.description: Italy's self-employment visa for non-EU nationals who wish to work as freelancers, independent professionals, or establish their own business under Italy's annual quota system (Decreto Flussi).
benefits: Work independently in Italy
Path to permanent residency
Schengen Area travel
Rich cultural environment
Access to Italian healthcare

visas.name: Italy Student Visa (Visto per Studio)
visas.description: Italy's student visa (Visto per Studio) for non-EU nationals who have been accepted into an Italian university, higher education institution, or accredited language school for stays over 90 days.
benefits: Study at world-class Italian universities
Part-time work permitted up to 20hrs/week
Schengen Area travel
Rich cultural experience
Pathway to post-study work permit

visas.name: Italy Short-Stay Schengen Visa (Type C)
visas.description: Italy's short-stay Schengen visa (Type C) allows non-EU nationals to visit Italy for tourism, business, or short courses for up to 90 days within a 180-day period.
benefits: Travel throughout the Schengen Area
Visit Italy for tourism or business
Quick processing
Straightforward application
Multiple entry options available

visas.name: Italy Investor Visa (Golden Visa)
visas.description: Italy's Investor Visa (Golden Visa) grants a 2-year residence permit to non-EU nationals who make a qualifying investment in Italian startups, companies, government bonds, or philanthropic projects.
benefits: EU residency
Schengen Area travel
Live and work in Italy
Family inclusion
Path to citizenship after 10 years

visas.description: For non-EU citizens who wish to live in Italy without working, supported by passive income or savings.

Path to EU residency
Healthcare access
Family inclusion
Schengen travel

Schengen access
Rich culture and lifestyle
Family inclusion
Path to residency

visas.name: Salaried Employment Visa (Visto per Lavoro Subordinato)
visas.description: The Salaried Employment Visa (Visto per Lavoro Subordinato) is for non-European Union citizens who have secured a job offer from an Italian employer. It allows the holder to enter Italy for long-term stay and engage in dependent work, leading to the issuance of a residence permit upon arrival.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens who have received a legitimate job offer from an Italian employer and obtained the prerequisite work authorization (Nulla Osta).
visas.path_to_residency_description: After a period of legal residence (typically 5 years) and work in Italy, holders of a salaried employment residence permit can apply for a long-term EU residence permit (Permesso di Soggiorno UE per soggiornanti di lungo periodo). This requires demonstrating stable and sufficient financial resources (at least the annual social security level), adequate accommodation, and not posing a threat to public order and security.
visas.renewal_conditions: To renew the residence permit, the holder must maintain employment, demonstrate sufficient financial resources, have adequate accommodation, and not have any criminal convictions. For long-term residency, an income equal to or higher than the annual social security level (e.g., €6,947.33 for 2024 for an individual) is required.
visas.tax_implications: Holders of this visa will generally be considered tax residents in Italy and subject to standard Italian income tax rules, including social security contributions (approx. 10% for employee, 30% for employer). No specific special tax treatments are mentioned for this visa category.
benefits: Permission to legally work in Italy under an employment contract.
Eligibility for a residence permit (Permesso di Soggiorno) upon arrival in Italy.
Provides a pathway to long-term residency in Italy.
Allows family reunification for eligible dependants.
required_documents: Duly completed and signed visa application form (Type D - National Visa).
Two recent passport-sized color photos (35x40mm, white/light background, I.C.A.O. standards).
Valid passport (valid for at least 3 months beyond visa expiry, with at least two blank pages).
Copy of the passport's first page and any previous Schengen visas with entry/exit stamps.
Original and copy of identity card (translated to Italian or English and legalized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Justice, if applicable).
Original Nulla Osta (work authorization letter) issued by the Sportello Unico per l'Immigrazione (SUI).
Confirmed flight reservation or air ticket.
Proof of accommodation in Italy (e.g., registered rental contract, hotel booking for at least 30 days, or a declaration of hospitality from a resident).
Signed employment contract specifying job title, salary, and employment conditions.
Educational certificates, diplomas, and professional qualification documents relevant to the job offer.

International medical insurance policy with a minimum coverage of EUR 30,000, including full and unlimited coverage for hospitalization, emergency repatriation flights, and repatriation of mortal remains.
Receipt of visa fee payment.
application_process_steps: The Italian employer applies for the Nulla Osta (work authorization) at the competent Sportello Unico per l'Immigrazione (SUI) in Italy, adhering to the annual 'Decreto Flussi' quotas for non-EU workers.
Upon approval, the SUI issues the Nulla Osta and electronically notifies the Italian Embassy or Consulate in the applicant's country of residence.

The applicant schedules an appointment and submits the Type D visa application, the original Nulla Osta, and all other required documents in person at the Italian Embassy or Consulate in their country of residence.
After entering Italy with the Salaried Employment Visa, the applicant must apply for a residence permit (Permesso di Soggiorno) at the Sportello Unico per l'Immigrazione (SUI) within 8 working days.

visas.name: Self-Employment Visa (Visto per Lavoro Autonomo)
visas.description: The 'Visto per Lavoro Autonomo' is a national Type D visa for non-EU citizens who wish to undertake non-occasional, authorized independent work in Italy, including freelance, professional, business, and entrepreneurial activities. It serves as an entry visa that allows applicants to obtain a residence permit upon arrival and live and work legally in Italy.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are non-EU citizens who are independent professionals, entrepreneurs, or individuals seeking to engage in self-employed activities in Italy, provided their work is properly authorized and non-occasional.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 5 years of continuous legal residence in Italy on a self-employment residence permit, applicants can apply for an EC long-term residence permit (permanent residency), provided they have sufficient financial resources, suitable accommodation, do not pose a threat to public order and security, and demonstrate A2 level Italian language proficiency. Italian citizenship can be applied for after 10 years of legal residence.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must continue the approved self-employed work, demonstrate sufficient income, and not be absent from Italy for more than 6 continuous months. Renewed annually, often for up to 2 years initially.
visas.tax_implications: If tax-resident in Italy, income from both Italian and foreign sources may be subject to Italian personal income tax (IRPEF). Non-residents are taxed only on Italian-source income. Double taxation treaties can provide relief. Small freelancers may be eligible for a simplified flat-rate tax regime ('regime forfettario') based on activity type and turnover. Social security contributions are mandatory to the Italian Social Security Administration (INPS) or a dedicated professional fund.
benefits: Ability to live and work legally as a self-employed individual in Italy.
Access to the Italian healthcare system (upon registration and contribution).
Allows for family reunification for dependants.
Path to permanent residency after 5 years and citizenship after 10 years.
Freedom of movement within the Schengen Area.
required_documents: Visa application form, completed and signed.
Recent passport-size color photo on a white background.
Valid passport (valid for at least 3 months beyond visa expiry, with at least 2 blank pages).
Proof of residence in the consular jurisdiction (e.g., driver's license, state ID).
Nulla Osta (entry clearance) issued by the competent Italian authority (Questura) within the last 90-180 days.
Proof of suitable accommodation in Italy (e.g., rental lease, ownership deed, or declaration of hospitality).
Proof of prior year's lawful income exceeding €8,400 (minimum for exemption from health services contributions).
Declaration from the local Chamber of Commerce or professional order attesting to sufficient economic resources for the intended activity (not less than €14,000).
Proof of professional qualifications, licenses, or registration with relevant professional bodies, if applicable.
Confirmed flight reservation (for visa application).
Health insurance covering medical expenses and hospitalization in Italy, often with a minimum €30,000 coverage and a repatriation clause.
application_process_steps: Obtain a 'Nulla Osta per Lavoro Autonomo' (no-impediment certificate) from the competent Italian authorities (e.g., Chamber of Commerce, Questura) in the province where the activity will be carried out. This often involves submitting a business plan and proof of qualifications and financial capacity while still abroad, usually through a legal representative.
Submit a Type D national visa application to the Italian Embassy or Consulate in your country of residence, including the Nulla Osta and all required supporting documents.
Enter Italy with the issued visa within 180 days of its issuance.

Within 8 days of arrival in Italy, apply for a 'Permesso di Soggiorno per Lavoro Autonomo' (residence permit for self-employment) at the local Questura (Police Headquarters) through the Post Office (Portale Immigrazione).
Attend a biometrics appointment and sign the Integration Agreement at the Immigration Office (Questura).
Collect the residence permit once issued.

visas.name: Digital Nomad / Remote Worker Visa (Visto per Nomadi Digitali / Lavoratori da Remoto)
visas.description: This visa is for non-EU citizens who wish to live in Italy while working remotely for an employer or clients based outside Italy. It allows individuals to immerse themselves in Italian culture and maintain their professional endeavors from within the country.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are highly skilled professionals (freelancers or employees of foreign companies) who can perform their work remotely using technological tools.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After entering Italy with the visa, applicants must apply for a 'Permesso di Soggiorno' (residence permit) at the local Questura within 8 working days. This permit is valid for one year and is renewable. After 5 years of continuous legal residence, applicants may qualify for a long-term EU residence permit, leading to potential Italian citizenship after 10 years.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must continue to meet original eligibility requirements, including income threshold, remote work status, accommodation, and health insurance. Renewed annually at the local Questura.
visas.tax_implications: Once considered an Italian tax resident (typically after 183 days in a calendar year), worldwide income is subject to Italian tax rules. No specific 'digital nomad tax' exists, but favorable tax regimes like the 'Regime Forfettario' (5% flat tax on a percentage of income for 5 years, if eligible, up to €85,000 revenue) or the 'Impatriates Tax Regime' (50-60% income exemption for high earners, with specific conditions including a 4-year commitment) may apply. Social security contributions are generally compulsory.
benefits: Allows long-term stay in Italy beyond the 90-day Schengen limit.
No requirement for a Nulla Osta (work permit) or annual immigration quotas.
Possibility to bring a spouse and minor children through family reunification.
Access to the Italian national health service (upon obtaining residence permit).
Clear path to permanent residency after 5 years and citizenship after 10 years.
required_documents: Valid passport (at least 15 months validity beyond intended travel, 2 blank pages)
National Visa application form (D-type)
One recent passport-sized photograph (ICAO standard)
Proof of physical residence in the consular jurisdiction (e.g., driver's license, utility bill)
Proof of legal residence in current country (for non-citizens of that country)
Travel medical insurance (min €30,000 coverage for medical expenses, hospitalization, repatriation)
Proof of highly qualified remote work (recognized degree, professional authorization, or relevant professional experience per Art. 27-quater)
Proof of at least six months of prior experience in the remote work field
Proof of stable, regular income (at least three times the minimum for healthcare exemption, e.g., paystubs, tax returns, bank statements)
Remote work contract or client agreements (for digital nomads) / Employer declaration (for remote workers)
Proof of accommodation in Italy (registered lease agreement or property deed for entire duration, not temporary bookings)
Clean criminal record certificate from country/countries of residence for the past 2 years (with apostille/legalization and sworn translation)
Self-certification stating no criminal convictions in the past five years (for freelancers)
application_process_steps: Assemble all required documents, ensuring translations and apostilles are obtained where necessary.
Book an appointment at the competent Italian Consulate or Embassy in your country of residence.
Submit the complete application package and pay the non-refundable visa application fee during the appointment.
Attend any required interview and provide biometric data at the consulate.
Wait for the visa approval; processing times can vary by consulate and applicant type.
Upon approval, enter Italy with the issued visa and apply for a 'Permesso di Soggiorno' at the local Questura within 8 working days of arrival.

visas.name: Elective Residency Visa (Visto per Residenza Elettiva)
visas.description: The Elective Residency Visa (Visto per Residenza Elettiva) is a long-stay visa for non-EU citizens who wish to live in Italy without engaging in any work activities. It is designed for individuals who can financially support themselves through stable, passive income and significant financial assets, choosing Italy as their country of permanent residence.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are financially independent individuals, such as retirees or those with substantial passive income from pensions, rental properties, investments, or other non-employment sources, who intend to reside permanently in Italy and do not plan to work.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After five years of continuous legal residency in Italy with a temporary residence permit, individuals may apply for a permanent residence permit. After ten years of legal residency with a permanent residence permit, eligibility for Italian citizenship by naturalization may be pursued, subject to language and integration requirements.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit is issued for one year and can be renewed annually, provided the holder continues to meet all original requirements, including maintaining the passive income threshold, suitable accommodation, and health insurance.
visas.tax_implications: Holders of the Elective Residency Visa who spend more than 183 days per year in Italy generally become Italian tax residents, meaning their worldwide passive income may be subject to Italian taxation, though this can be influenced by tax treaties.
benefits: Long-term legal residence in Italy.
Ability to purchase or rent residential property in Italy.
Freedom to travel within the Schengen Area.
Path to permanent residency after 5 years and Italian citizenship after 10 years.
Possibility to include a spouse and dependent children on the visa.
required_documents: Completed long-stay visa application form.
Valid passport (valid for at least three months beyond the visa's expiration, with two blank pages).
Recent passport-sized photographs (meeting Schengen requirements).
Proof of substantial and stable passive income (e.g., pension statements, rental income, investment returns, annuities, bank letters).
Proof of suitable accommodation in Italy (registered lease agreement or property deed for a minimum of one year).
Private health insurance policy covering at least €30,000 for medical expenses in the Schengen area.
Letter explaining the reasons for moving to Italy, intended length of stay, and accommodation details.
Civil status documents (e.g., marriage certificates, birth certificates for dependents), if applicable.
Tax returns for the last 1-2 years (often requested).
FBI background check or criminal certificate (may be required by some consulates).
application_process_steps: Determine the correct Italian Consulate based on your place of residence and schedule a visa appointment.
Gather all required documentation, ensuring all financial and accommodation proofs meet the specified criteria.
Attend the in-person visa interview at the consulate, submitting all original documents and paying the application fee.
Wait for the visa application to be processed by the consulate.
Upon approval, the visa will be affixed in your passport, allowing entry into Italy.
Within 8 days of arriving in Italy, apply for a Permesso di Soggiorno (residence permit) at the local Police Department (Questura).

visas.name: Investor Visa for Italy (Golden Visa)
visas.description: The Investor Visa for Italy, also known as the Golden Visa, is a residency-by-investment program designed for non-EU/EEA/Swiss citizens. It allows individuals to obtain a two-year Italian residence permit by making a significant financial contribution to the Italian economy, with options including investment in government bonds, Italian companies, innovative startups, or philanthropic donations.
visas.target_applicant: This visa is ideal for high-net-worth individuals and entrepreneurs from outside the EU/EEA/Switzerland who are looking to gain residency in Italy through a qualifying investment, without stringent physical presence requirements.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After five years of legal and continuous residence in Italy, Investor Visa holders may apply for an EU long-term residence permit (permanent residency). Citizenship by naturalization may be available after ten years of continuous legal residence (183 days per year), subject to language proficiency (minimum A2 level) and other legal requirements.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit is initially valid for two years and can be renewed for a further three years, provided the qualifying investment is maintained. A new Nulla Osta from the Investor Visa Committee is required for renewal, and applicants must apply at least 60 days before the expiry date. Clean criminal record and health insurance are also required for renewal.
visas.tax_implications: Italy offers a special optional tax regime for new residents, allowing them to pay a flat €300,000 per year instead of regular taxes on foreign-sourced income. This regime, increased by the 2026 Budget Law, can last up to 15 years, with an additional flat tax of €50,000 per year for each qualifying family member. To qualify, individuals must move their tax residence to Italy and not have been resident in Italy for at least 9 out of the last 10 years. This regime also provides exemptions from wealth taxes on foreign assets and non-reporting of foreign assets.
benefits: Initial 2-year residence permit, renewable for three more years, with a clear path to long-term residency and citizenship.
Visa-free travel within the Schengen Area.
Right to live, work, and study in Italy.
Ability to include immediate family members (spouse and dependent children) in the application.
Access to a special flat tax regime for new residents on foreign-sourced income.
required_documents: Duly completed application form.
Valid passport or travel document (valid for at least two years with at least two blank pages).
Recent passport-style photograph (full front, white background, not older than 6 months).
Nulla Osta (pre-approval certificate) issued by the Investor Visa for Italy Committee.
Professional résumé/CV.
Criminal background checks from countries of residence for the past 10 years, apostilled and translated.
Documentation proving the chosen investment type, source, and availability of funds, and commitment to invest.
Proof of legal ownership and lawful origin of funds (anti-money laundering declaration).
Proof of sufficient financial resources beyond the investment for self-sufficiency.
Valid health insurance for Italy (required at visa stage and for renewal).
application_process_steps: Create a personal account and submit an online application to the Investor Visa Committee (IV4I) via the official portal, including CV, contact details, proposed investment, and required attachments.
The Committee Secretariat reviews the application and issues a Nulla Osta (pre-approval certificate) within 30 days if approved.
Applicants have six months from the Nulla Osta issuance to apply for the investor visa in person at the Italian Consulate in their country of residence.
Upon visa approval, enter Italy. The investment must be completed within three months of arrival.
Within eight days of arriving in Italy, apply for a residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) at the local police station (Questura).
Upload proof of the completed investment on the Investor-Visa portal and provide biometric data at the Questura.

visas.name: Family Reunification Visa (Visto per Ricongiungimento Familiare)
visas.description: The Italy Family Reunification Visa (Visto per Ricongiungimento Familiare) allows non-EU family members to join a foreign citizen who is legally residing in Italy. It facilitates the exercise of the right to family unity, enabling family members to live, work, and study in Italy with their loved ones.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens who are close family members (spouse, minor children, dependent adult children with specific conditions, dependent parents) of a foreign national legally residing in Italy with an appropriate residence permit for at least one year, or in some cases, of an Italian/EU citizen.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After five years of continuous legal residence in Italy, and upon registering as a tax resident and demonstrating an A2 level of Italian language proficiency, visa holders may apply for a permanent residence permit.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit for family reunification has the same duration as the sponsor's residence permit and is renewable, provided the requirements for entry into the territory continue to be met.
benefits: Legally live together in Italy, eliminating reliance on short-term or tourist visas
Adults can work and children can integrate into the Italian school system
Access to Italy's public healthcare system
Eligibility for social support, such as parental benefits or support for dependents with special needs
Path to apply for a permanent residence permit after five years of continuous legal residence
required_documents: Nulla Osta (clearance/authorization) issued by the Sportello Unico Immigrazione (SUI) in Italy, valid for six months
National Visa Application Form, duly completed and signed
Valid passport with at least two blank pages and validity of at least 3 months beyond the visa's expiration, plus a photocopy of the personal data page
Two recent passport-sized photographs (3cm x 4cm), white background, identical
Documentation proving the family relationship (e.g., original marriage certificate for spouse, birth certificate for children), legalized and translated into Italian
Proof of suitable accommodation in Italy that complies with health and hygiene requirements

Proof of adequate financial means to support the family members, such as recent Italian tax returns, pay slips, and bank statements. The annual income must not be less than the social allowance for each family member to be reunited (double the social allowance for two or more children under 14)
Copy of the sponsor's valid Italian Residence Permit (Permesso di Soggiorno) and passport
For minors, a notarized consent form from the other parent for permanent transfer of residence to Italy
For dependent parents or adult children, proof of dependency and/or documented severe disability
Letter of invitation from the Italian/EU citizen (for family members of EU citizens) stating the intention to exercise the right to family unity, accompanied by a valid ID
Proof of economic remittances (for dependent parents of EU citizens, where dependency is assessed)
application_process_steps: The sponsor (foreign citizen residing in Italy) must have resided legally and continuously in Italy for at least two years.
The sponsor applies for the 'Nulla Osta' (authorization for family reunification) online through the Unified Immigration Desk (Sportello Unico per l'Immigrazione – SUI) in their province.

The SUI verifies the requirements, including the sponsor's income, accommodation, and absence of criminal impediments, and issues the Nulla Osta within 150 days. The Nulla Osta is valid for six months.

The family member abroad applies for the entry visa (Visto per Ricongiungimento Familiare) at the competent Italian consulate or embassy in their country of residence, submitting the original Nulla Osta and other required documentation.
The consulate or embassy verifies the family relationship and issues the visa within 30 days of application, if approved.

Upon entering Italy with the visa, the family member must apply for a Residence Permit (Permesso di Soggiorno) at the One-Stop-Shop for Immigration (Prefettura) via the Post Office within eight working days.

visas.name: EU Blue Card (Carta Blu UE)
visas.description: The EU Blue Card (Carta Blu UE) program in Italy is a residence and work permit for highly qualified non-EU citizens. It facilitates their entry and stay in Italy for highly skilled employment, offering a streamlined process compared to general work permits.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens who possess a higher education qualification or relevant professional experience, and have a binding job offer in Italy for a highly qualified position meeting specific salary thresholds.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 5 years of legal residence in the EU (at least 2 of which must be in Italy), the holder can apply for long-term EU resident status.
benefits: Not subject to the annual Decreto Flussi (quota system), allowing year-round application.
Grants the right to live and work in Italy.
Allows for family reunification with simplified procedures for spouses and children.
Provides access to public services and social security.
After 18 months, allows for easier mobility to another EU Member State under the Blue Card scheme.
Offers a clear path to long-term EU resident status.
required_documents: Valid travel document (passport)

Higher education qualification (tertiary level, at least 3 years of study) or equivalent professional qualification (at least 5 years of relevant professional experience, or 3 years for ICT managers/specialists acquired within the last 7 years)
Declaration of Value (Dichiarazione di Valore) for foreign degrees or CIMEA attestation (if applicable)
Valid work contract or binding job offer for highly qualified employment with a duration of at least 6 months
Proof of sickness insurance (or application for it)
Proof of accommodation in Italy (including cadastral details)
Application for a visa (if necessary, after Nulla Osta issuance)
Tax stamp (€16)
4 passport-sized photos with white background
application_process_steps: Employer submits the Nulla Osta (work permit clearance) application online to the local Sportello Unico per l'Immigrazione (SUI) through the Ministry of Interior's portal.
SUI evaluates the application, obtains necessary opinions from Questura and Direzione Territoriale del Lavoro.
If approved, SUI issues the Nulla Osta to the employer (maximum 90 days processing).
Applicant applies for an entry visa (D visa for highly qualified work) at the Italian Embassy or Consulate in their country of residence.
Upon entering Italy, the applicant must report to the SUI within 8 working days to sign the 'contratto di soggiorno' (contract of stay).
The applicant then applies for the Carta Blu UE residence permit at the Questura (Police Headquarters) via a postal kit.
The Questura issues the electronic Carta Blu UE residence permit.

visas.name: Startup Visa
visas.description: The Italy Startup Visa program is designed for non-EU entrepreneurs and innovators who intend to establish a new innovative startup in Italy or join an existing one. It offers a streamlined immigration route to foster economic growth and technological advancement in the country.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens with an innovative business idea or the intention to join an innovative Italian startup as a founder, shareholder, or director.
visas.path_to_residency_description: The initial visa grants a 1-year residence permit, which is renewable. After 10 years of legal residence in Italy, applicants may be eligible to apply for Italian citizenship.
visas.renewal_conditions: The company must be effectively incorporated in Italy, registered in the Special Section of the Companies Register as an innovative startup, and continue to meet all statutory and economic requirements. Innovative startup status can be extended up to 9 years based on revenue growth, investment rounds, technological development, and employment expansion.
visas.tax_implications: Italy offers several tax incentives for innovative startups and foreign entrepreneurs, including the Smart&Start Italia funding program, R&D tax credits, investor tax deductions, access to the SME Guarantee Fund, and regional startup incentives. Eligible individuals may also benefit from the inbound worker tax regime.
benefits: Fast-track approval process for the Nulla Osta (clearance certificate)
Exemption from annual immigration quotas ('Decreto Flussi')
Lower capital requirements compared to other investor visas
Access to EU residence and the EU single market
Potential for long-term residency and citizenship pathway
Entitlement to live and work in Italy while developing the startup
Access to various tax incentives and funding programs for innovative startups
required_documents: Completed visa application form
Recent passport-sized photographs
Valid passport
Proof of financial resources (bank statements, bank letters, anti-money laundering statement) demonstrating at least €50,000 for a new startup, or often higher for joining an existing one
A detailed business plan explaining the innovative startup concept, business model, goods/services, technological aspects, and target market
Curriculum Vitae (CV) and professional experience relevant to the startup project
Nulla Osta (certificate of no impediment) issued by the Italia Startup Visa Committee
Proof of suitable accommodation in Italy (e.g., hotel booking, rental agreement)
Certificate of minimum income for the previous financial year (at least €8,500)
Cover letter explaining the business idea and startup plans
application_process_steps: Submit the online application for the Nulla Osta (clearance certificate) to the Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy (MIMIT) committee, including the business plan, CVs, and financial documentation.
Await evaluation by the MIMIT Technical Committee and receive the Nulla Osta upon approval.
Apply for a Type D national self-employment visa (Italia Startup Visa) at the competent Italian Embassy or Consulate in the applicant's country of residence.
After entering Italy with the visa, apply for a 1-year residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) at the local police headquarters (Questura).

Citizenship by Descent.desc:
Italian citizenship by descent (jure sanguinis) is recognized, meaning it's based on the 'right of blood.' As of May 24, 2025, due to Law 74/2025 (Tajani Decree), new stricter eligibility rules apply:
*   Applicants can now only claim citizenship through a parent or grandparent (no longer great-grandparents or earlier generations).
*   The Italian parent or grandparent must have held *exclusively* Italian citizenship at the time of the applicant's birth, or at the time of their death if they died before the applicant's birth.
*   There must be an unbroken bloodline between the applicant and their Italian-born ancestor.
*   Prior to March 17, 1861, there were no Italian citizens, so the oldest Italian ancestor must have been alive on or after this date.
*   For claims through a female Italian ancestor, the child must have been born on or after January 1, 1948. While this restriction has been successfully overturned in Italian courts, consulates and municipal offices are still required to apply it unless a court case (1948 case) is pursued.
*   Italian citizenship was exclusive until August 15, 1992; voluntary acquisition of another nationality before this date meant automatic renunciation of Italian citizenship, which could break the bloodline for descendants born before August 16, 1992.
*   Children under 18 can be recognized if at least one parent is an Italian citizen and declares the intention for recognition, provided the child's birth is registered or they resided in Italy for at least two consecutive years.

Naturalization.desc:
Naturalization based on residency generally requires a period of legal residence in Italy.
*   For non-EU citizens, the standard requirement is 10 years of legal residency.
*   This period is reduced to 3 years for individuals of Italian descent (e.g., those with Italian-born parents or grandparents) and for stateless persons.
*   EU citizens generally require 4 years of legal residency.
*   Applicants must demonstrate a sufficient knowledge of the Italian language, typically at a B1 level or higher, by passing a language test.

Birthright.desc:
Italy's citizenship law is primarily based on *jus sanguinis* (right of blood), with *jus soli* (right of soil/birthright) applied only in exceptional circumstances.
*   Children born in Italy automatically acquire Italian citizenship at birth if at least one parent is an Italian citizen.
*   Individuals born in Italy to non-Italian parents who do not acquire the citizenship of their parents (e.g., due to parents being stateless or of unknown nationality) and would otherwise be stateless automatically acquire Italian citizenship at birth.
*   Foreigners born in Italy who have resided in Italy from birth to the age of 18 without interruption may apply for citizenship upon reaching adulthood.

Spouse and Family.desc:
Non-Italian spouses of Italian citizens can apply for Italian citizenship through marriage (jure matrimonii).
*   **For couples residing in Italy:** The non-Italian spouse is eligible after two years of marriage or civil union.
*   **For couples residing outside Italy:** The waiting period is three years from the date of marriage or civil union.
*   **Reduction for children:** These waiting periods are reduced by half if the couple has biological or adopted children under 18 years of age.
*   **Language Requirement:** Applicants must demonstrate Italian language proficiency at a B1 level or higher.
*   **Marriage Registration:** The marriage must be transcribed into Italian civil records before a citizenship application can be submitted.
*   **Processing Time:** The Ministry of Interior generally processes applications within a maximum of 36 months (3 years) from formal acceptance.
*   **Historical Note:** Foreign women who married Italian men before April 27, 1983, automatically acquired Italian citizenship.
*   **Same-sex Civil Unions:** Same-sex civil unions, recognized in Italy since 2016, qualify for this citizenship pathway, with foreign same-sex marriages treated equivalently.

tax_advice:
*   **Personal Income Tax (IRPEF):** Italy taxes residents on worldwide income with progressive rates. As of 2026, IRPEF uses three brackets: 23% on income up to €28,000, 35% on €28,001–€50,000, and 43% above €50,000. Regional surtaxes (1.23–3.33%) and municipal surtaxes (up to 0.9%) are added.
*   **Corporate Tax:** The standard corporate income tax rate (IRES) is generally 24%. Regional tax on productive activities (IRAP) also applies, typically around 3.9% (though it can vary by region and activity).
*   **VAT (Imposta sul Valore Aggiunto - IVA):** The standard VAT rate in Italy is 22%. Reduced rates of 10%, 5%, and 4% apply to specific goods and services (e.g., certain foods, medicines, e-books), and a 0% rate applies to intra-community and international transport and medical care.
*   **Expat Tax Incentives:**
    *   **Impatriate Regime (Regime degli Impatriati):** For workers transferring tax residency to Italy, this regime offers a 50% income exemption for 5 years (60% if at least one minor child is present). The benefit applies up to a €600,000 annual income cap. To qualify, one must not have been tax resident in Italy for the preceding 3 tax periods.
    *   **Flat Tax for Wealthy New Residents (Art. 24-bis TUIR):** As of January 1, 2026, qualifying new residents can opt to pay a fixed annual substitute tax of €300,000 on all foreign-sourced income, regardless of the amount. A charge of €50,000 per year applies for accompanying family members. This regime applies for up to 15 years, requiring prior non-residence for 9 of the 10 preceding tax years. Italian-sourced income is taxed normally.
    *   **7% Retiree Tax Regime:** Foreign pensioners moving to eligible Southern Italian towns with less than 30,000 inhabitants can benefit from a 7% flat tax on all foreign-sourced income for up to 10 years.
*   **Social Security:** Employee social security contributions (INPS) are approximately 9.19% of gross salary.
local_tips:
*   **Cost of Living:** Italy is generally more affordable than many other Western European countries and the US, though costs vary widely by region. A single person might expect to spend €1,600–€2,300 per month in a mid-sized city, or €2,000–€2,700 in more expensive Northern cities like Milan and Rome, including rent. A family of four could range from €3,200–€4,000 in cheaper Southern regions to €3,800–€4,800 in major Northern urban hubs. Rent is the biggest factor, with Milan and Rome being the most expensive.
*   **Language:** While English is spoken in international business and tourist areas, learning Italian is essential for daily life, social integration, and navigating bureaucracy outside major cities.
*   **Safety:** Italy is generally safe, with violent crime being rare. Petty crimes like pickpocketing and bag snatching are common, especially in tourist areas. Naples is cited as having a lower safety index compared to Florence, Milan, and Rome.
*   **Registration:** Within 8 days of arriving in Italy with a visa, expats must apply for a Permesso di Soggiorno (residency permit) at a local post office to formalize their legal stay. Registering your marriage in Italian civil records is a prerequisite for citizenship by marriage applications.
*   **Bureaucracy:** Italian bureaucracy is frequently cited as complex, slow, and frustrating, requiring significant patience and often professional assistance for administrative tasks, visa processes, and utility setup.
*   **Healthcare:** Residents gain access to Italy's national health service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale - SSN), which is well-regarded globally. Private healthcare options are also available.
